slides.title: First, reproduce learning in a simpler setting.
slides.notes: The immediate aim is to reproduce a known language-model learning recipe. Math gives us an answer we can check. Recursive choices come later. This is a small reproduction, not a new method or a reproduction of the paper's headline scores.

slides.title: Reward correct attempts, then change the model.
slides.notes: This example is invented. The model generates its own attempts. The checker supplies only final-answer scores. Relative scores guide weight updates. We use eight attempts per question. If all eight scores agree, there is no within-question learning signal.

slides.title: We train on math, then test on different questions.
slides.notes: The main run started from the base model: 512 questions, eight attempts each, 32 updates. The 128 test questions were excluded from training and monitoring. We cannot rule out earlier pretraining exposure. No worked-solution SFT stage was added.

slides.title: Training improved answers on the separate test.
slides.notes: Fixed test: 41 to 80 correct out of 128. There were 44 gains and five losses. Same prompts and checker. We used the final checkpoint, not the best. This is one training run. More test questions cannot replace an independent training repeat.

slides.title: A higher score does not always mean a new skill.
slides.notes: Actual test row 5: repeated fraction question became a correct 0.15. Responses are summarized. Of 44 gains, 36 started as capped responses. That describes the change, not its cause. Prompt controls are pending. Math gains do not establish better RLM decomposition.
